sourceCheck: Pin: Node.js 24.21.0, Active LTS on 2026-10-08. The successful pinned API pages identify themselves as Node.js v24.21.0 Documentation. Node.js 22.23.3 is Maintenance LTS, with EOL scheduled for 2027-04-30. Node.js 24 enters Maintenance on 2026-10-20 and reaches EOL on 2028-04-30. Node.js 26.11.0 is Current, with Active LTS scheduled for 2026-10-28, Maintenance for 2027-10-20, and EOL for 2029-04-30. These schedule dates are subject to change. Sources opened: https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases, https://github.com/nodejs/Release, https://github.com/nodejs/Release/blob/main/schedule.json, https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/evolving-the-nodejs-release-schedule and https://nodejs.org/dist/index.json. The distribution index confirms v26.11.0 dated 2026-10-07 with V8 14.6, v24.21.0 dated 2026-09-07 with V8 13.6, and v22.23.3 dated 2026-09-23. The v27 schedule lists Alpha on 2026-10-28, Current on 2027-04-22, maintenance on 2027-10-20 and EOL on 2030-04-30, with no lts date or codename. The announcement's illustrative April 2026 entry for v26 differs from its actual initial release on 2026-05-05; exact dates follow the schedule and release records. API access: https://nodejs.org/api/ currently lists Current-line .md and .json files dated 07-Oct-2026, rather than serving the pinned 24 HTML documentation. Its process.html returned 404. Attempts to open latest-v26.x, v26.11.0 and the suggested v26.10.0 HTML fallback were inaccessible through the browser tool; those tool failures are not independently established HTTP 404s. Exact v26.11.0 doc/api sources were fetched from GitHub instead. Under https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/, documentation.html, process.html, dns.html, fs.html, buffer.html, http.html, crypto.html, worker_threads.html, typescript.html and test.html opened successfully. cli.html, modules.html, esm.html, packages.html, module.html, permissions.html, events.html, stream.html, path.html, child_process.html, timers.html, errors.html, globals.html and deprecations.html were attempted but inaccessible through the browser tool; their exact v24.21.0 doc/api sources were fetched and read. All these API subjects were compared with exact v26.11.0 sources at https://github.com/nodejs/node/tree/v26.11.0/doc/api. Also read the Version 26.0.0 notable changes in https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/changelogs/CHANGELOG_V26.md. All eleven requested Learn guides opened: https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick, https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/understanding-processnexttick, https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/understanding-setimmediate, https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop, https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/overview-of-blocking-vs-non-blocking, https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/the-nodejs-event-emitter, https://nodejs.org/learn/modules/how-to-use-streams, https://nodejs.org/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams, https://nodejs.org/learn/typescript/run-natively, https://nodejs.org/learn/command-line/how-to-read-environment-variables-from-nodejs and https://nodejs.org/learn/test-runner/introduction. Scoped differences: --experimental-transform-types exists in 24 at Stability 1.2 and was removed in 26.0.0. The 26 Permission Model additionally restricts network access and FFI and suppresses the SIGUSR1 inspector listener; --allow-net is absent from 24. The 26 filesystem permission section denies descriptor-based fsync, fdatasync, fchmod and fchown operations, including corresponding synchronous and FileHandle APIs, with ERR_ACCESS_DENIED. Its Caveats nevertheless retain the broad existing-descriptor bypass claim also present in 24, creating an internal contradiction. module.register() has documentation-only DEP0205 in 24 and runtime DEP0205 in 26. The deprecated process multipleResolves event is present in 24 and absent in 26. Buffer.stringLength() and alignment arguments for Buffer.allocUnsafe() and Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow() appear in 26 only; SlowBuffer is removed there. Recursive fs.rmdir() and top-level fs.F_OK, R_OK, W_OK and X_OK are runtime-deprecated in 24 and removed in 26. The fs.glob() family gains maxDepth in 26; fsPromises.watch() documents overflow 'throw' in 24 versus 'error' in 26. Node.js 26 adds the DEP0209 child-process signal cleanup note, elaborates Worker permission inheritance and transferable socket documentation, and clarifies asynchronous signal delivery. Its errors page expands DOMException documentation without changing the Node.js error.code rule. events.addAbortListener() gains behavior for the event argument and cancellation of a pending listener when the signal is already aborted; that API is outside the card plan. Temporal is enabled by default in 26 and disabled by default in 24. Both lines document OpenSSL STORE permission restrictions, beyond the original resource list. These differences and excluded APIs receive no cards. Source conflicts: both crypto pages claim a repeated hmac.digest() throws, but DEP0206 in both release lines says it returns an empty buffer; the 24 deprecation was added in 24.18.0. Repeated Hmac digest behavior is excluded. The Learn TypeScript guide retains older flag names and recommends TypeScript 5.7, whereas the API uses --no-strip-types and recommends 5.8. The Learn environment guide still labels .env support experimental, whereas the pinned APIs mark --env-file and process.loadEnvFile() stable. The event loop Learn guide recommends setImmediate() universally, whereas process.html favors queueMicrotask() for most userland deferrals and marks process.nextTick() Legacy. The shorter nextTick guide's general priority wording omits the ES module microtask context; process.html controls ordering cards. The setImmediate guide uses queue terminology and general iteration wording that the cards replace with the API's phase and scheduling rules. The Don't Block guide additionally lists dns.lookupService(), while cli.html lists dns.lookup(); lookupService receives no card. Both stream Learn guides overgeneralize when a busy queue causes write() to return false, and the backpressure guide describes highWaterMark as a limit; stream.html specifies threshold behavior. The Release README's generic odd-numbered and twice-yearly release paragraphs describe the model through 26, while the announcement and Previous Releases page establish the annual model beginning with 27. The packages page also retains a shorthand CommonJS description for missing type metadata; its explicit syntax-detection section supplies the exception. The remaining requested behaviors support the plan. Every b1 verdict agrees across Node.js 24 and 26.

cards.statement: Node.js runs JavaScript callbacks on one event loop thread.
cards.explanation: One thread executes callbacks for the main event loop.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop — callback execution

cards.statement: Node.js uses libuv to implement its Worker Pool.
cards.explanation: libuv supplies the pool that executes native tasks.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop — Worker Pool

cards.statement: Node.js assigns non-blocking network I/O to libuv's threadpool.
cards.explanation: Node.js uses the operating system's asynchronous network interfaces.
cards.misconception: Asynchronous network operations consume threadpool workers.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop — network I/O

cards.statement: fs.readFile() with a callback uses libuv's threadpool for its file operations.
cards.explanation: libuv workers perform the file operations used by asynchronous fs.readFile().

cards.statement: dns.lookup() runs a synchronous getaddrinfo() call on libuv's threadpool.
cards.explanation: The asynchronous API delegates the blocking system call to a worker.

cards.statement: dns.resolve4() consults /etc/hosts when resolving a host name.
cards.explanation: dns.resolve4() queries DNS servers and ignores /etc/hosts.
cards.misconception: The DNS resolver API incorporates local hosts-file entries.

cards.statement: crypto.pbkdf2() with a callback computes its result on the event loop thread.
cards.explanation: The asynchronous crypto.pbkdf2() computation runs in libuv's threadpool.
cards.misconception: The event loop performs the asynchronous key-derivation computation.

cards.statement: Asynchronous zlib compression uses libuv's threadpool to perform the compression work.
cards.explanation: libuv workers execute zlib operations submitted by the asynchronous API.

cards.statement: Assigning process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in user code reliably resizes libuv's threadpool.
cards.explanation: Setting UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE inside the process is not guaranteed to work.
cards.misconception: Changing the environment variable during execution reliably changes the pool.

cards.statement: fs.readFileSync() blocks the event loop while it reads a file.
cards.explanation: Other event loop callbacks wait for the synchronous read to finish.

cards.statement: Node.js moves JSON.parse() of a large string to its Worker Pool.
cards.explanation: JSON.parse() executes on the calling JavaScript thread.
cards.misconception: Node.js automatically offloads expensive JSON parsing.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop — JSON DOS

cards.statement: A slow crypto task in libuv's threadpool affects just the other crypto tasks.
cards.explanation: Unrelated operations sharing the pool can also slow down.
cards.misconception: Threadpool contention remains isolated within the originating core module.

cards.statement: Node.js runs the timers phase before poll in each event loop iteration.
cards.explanation: Iteration timers run after poll; an initial timer pass precedes the loop.
cards.misconception: The initial timer pass also describes the recurring iteration order.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — phase overview

cards.statement: An event loop phase processes its callback queue in last-in, first-out order.
cards.explanation: Phase callback queues use first-in, first-out order.
cards.misconception: Event loop phase queues behave like stacks.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — phase queues

cards.statement: Node.js uses the idle and prepare phases for internal work.
cards.explanation: These phases serve Node.js internals.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — phase overview

cards.statement: The pending callbacks phase runs I/O callbacks deferred from the previous iteration.
cards.explanation: Some system-operation callbacks wait until this phase.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — pending callbacks

cards.statement: The poll phase calculates how long Node.js should wait for I/O.
cards.explanation: Poll determines its waiting duration before processing available events.

cards.statement: An empty poll queue keeps waiting for I/O when setImmediate() callbacks are queued.
cards.explanation: Queued immediates let poll end its wait.
cards.misconception: Pending immediates leave poll's I/O wait unchanged.

cards.statement: The check phase runs each callback scheduled by setImmediate().
cards.explanation: Node.js invokes immediate callbacks during check.

cards.statement: Node.js emits an abruptly closed socket's 'close' event in the close callbacks phase.
cards.explanation: Abrupt handle closure uses the close callbacks phase.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — close callbacks

cards.statement: setTimeout() schedules its callback for the exact instant its delay expires.
cards.explanation: The delay is a minimum threshold; other work can postpone execution.
cards.misconception: A timer delay guarantees an exact execution time.

cards.statement: Node.js normally exits once its event loop becomes empty.
cards.explanation: An empty event loop normally lets the process terminate.

cards.statement: timeout.unref() cancels the timeout's scheduled callback.
cards.explanation: unref() changes whether the timer keeps the process alive.
cards.misconception: Removing a timer's reference cancels its work.

cards.statement: A timeout starts in an unreferenced state by default.
cards.explanation: Timeout objects initially keep the event loop alive.
cards.misconception: New timeouts require an explicit reference to keep the process running.

cards.statement: The poll phase runs the callbacks stored in the next tick queue.
cards.explanation: The next tick queue is processed outside the loop's phases.
cards.misconception: The next tick queue belongs to the poll phase.

cards.statement: process.nextTick() defers its callback until the current JavaScript operation finishes.
cards.explanation: The current operation finishes before its queued next tick callbacks run.

cards.statement: In ES module top-level code, queueMicrotask() callbacks precede process.nextTick() callbacks queued there.
cards.explanation: ES module evaluation already runs inside the microtask queue.

cards.statement: A setImmediate() callback queued inside another immediate runs in the same event loop iteration.
cards.explanation: Node.js defers the nested immediate to the next iteration.
cards.misconception: An executing immediate's new immediate joins the current iteration.

cards.statement: The Node.js docs favor queueMicrotask() over process.nextTick() for most userland deferrals.
cards.explanation: The API docs recommend queueMicrotask() for portable deferred execution.

cards.statement: process.nextTick(callback, value) passes value to the deferred callback.
cards.explanation: Arguments following the callback reach that callback when Node.js invokes it.

cards.statement: Recursive process.nextTick() calls give the poll phase a turn between queued callbacks.
cards.explanation: The next tick queue can keep refilling and starve I/O.
cards.misconception: Recursive next tick scheduling regularly yields to I/O.

cards.statement: The main CommonJS module gives setTimeout(fn, 0) callbacks priority over setImmediate(fn) callbacks.
cards.explanation: Their order in the main CommonJS module depends on runtime timing.
cards.misconception: A zero-delay timeout has a fixed scheduling priority in the main module.

cards.statement: Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate(fn) runs before setTimeout(fn, 0) when both are scheduled there.
cards.explanation: An immediate scheduled during I/O precedes the zero-delay timeout.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — immediate versus timeout

cards.statement: setTimeout() from node:timers/promises fulfills its promise with the supplied value.
cards.explanation: The optional value becomes the promise's fulfillment result.

cards.statement: An EventEmitter's synchronous constructor emit reaches a listener attached after construction.
cards.explanation: A later listener misses the event already emitted during construction.
cards.misconception: Constructor events remain available to listeners attached afterward.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop — constructor event example

cards.statement: Aborting a pending node:timers/promises timeout via its supplied signal fulfills the promise early.
cards.explanation: Cancelling with AbortSignal rejects the timer promise with AbortError.
cards.misconception: Cancelling a promise timer counts as successful early completion.

cards.statement: By default, Node.js loads a .mjs file as an ES module in a package with "type": "commonjs".
cards.explanation: The .mjs extension determines the file's module format.

cards.statement: Node.js takes a .js file's "type" from the project's root package.json despite a nearer package.json.
cards.explanation: The nearest parent package.json supplies the controlling type field.
cards.misconception: Project-root metadata overrides a nested package's module format.

cards.statement: An import() expression makes an ambiguous .js file qualify as an ES module during syntax detection.
cards.explanation: Dynamic import() is valid in CommonJS, so it is not a detection marker.
cards.misconception: Any import syntax selects ES module interpretation for ambiguous input.
cards.volatilityNote: Syntax detection is documented at Stability 1.2, release candidate.

cards.statement: The packages docs recommend an explicit "type" field even for packages whose sources are CommonJS.
cards.explanation: Explicit type metadata makes module interpretation predictable.

source.title: Packages — determining module system, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: node --input-type=module --eval treats its supplied source string as an ES module.
cards.explanation: The flag selects the module format for string input.

source.title: Packages — input type flag, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: Node.js resolves `import './utils'` to ./utils/index.js when utils is a directory.
cards.explanation: A directory index import needs the complete path, including index.js.
cards.misconception: Relative ES module imports automatically resolve directory index files.

source.title: ES modules — mandatory file extensions, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: In a CommonJS module, Node.js requires the node: prefix to load the built-in test runner.
cards.explanation: The built-in test runner is addressed as node:test.

source.title: CommonJS modules — mandatory node: prefix, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: Node.js derives CommonJS named exports for ES module imports by evaluating the module's export object.
cards.explanation: Node.js detects these names through heuristic static analysis.
cards.misconception: Node.js discovers named CommonJS exports from the evaluated object's properties.

source.title: ES modules — CommonJS namespaces, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: In a .cjs file, require() waits for an ES module dependency's top-level await before returning.
cards.explanation: Top-level await anywhere in the graph triggers ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE.
cards.misconception: Synchronous require() waits for asynchronous ES module initialization.

source.title: CommonJS modules — require() of ES modules, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: In a .cjs file, require() of a .mjs file with `export default 7` returns a namespace with .default equal to 7.
cards.explanation: The default export occupies the namespace's default property.

source.title: CommonJS modules — require() namespace result, v24.21.0 source

cards.statement: module.createRequire(import.meta.url) supplies a require function inside an ES module.
cards.explanation: Node.js anchors the returned require function to the supplied file URL.

cards.statement: A data: ES module exposes import.meta.dirname as its containing directory.
cards.explanation: import.meta.dirname is provided for modules using the file: protocol.
cards.misconception: Node.js provides filesystem directory metadata for data: modules.
